name: Vitamin E
summary: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin that protects the fats in cell membranes from damage. Real shortage is rare and mostly affects people who can't absorb fat. Large trials of vitamin E supplements didn't prevent heart disease or cancer, and some found harm.
roles: Antioxidant that protects fats in cell membranes and in blood fats (lipoproteins) from damage

status.note: The test is blood (plasma or serum) alpha-tocopherol. It rises and falls with blood fats (cholesterol and triglycerides), which carry it, so it is best read alongside them or as a ratio to them. A clearly low value (below about 12 µmol/L) points to shortage, but a normal value doesn't prove the tissues have enough. It is rarely tested except in conditions with poor fat absorption. This app has no vitamin E marker yet.

signs: Nerve damage: numbness, poor balance and coordination (ataxia), loss of the sense of where the limbs are
Damage to the retina at the back of the eye
Breakdown of red blood cells (haemolysis), mainly in premature babies
atRisk: People who absorb fat poorly: cystic fibrosis, long-standing liver or bile duct disease, Crohn's disease, short bowel, after some weight-loss operations
People with a rare inherited condition that stops the liver passing vitamin E into the blood (ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, AVED)
Premature babies with very low birth weight

signs: Easy bruising and bleeding, such as nosebleeds or bleeding gums
More bleeding strokes (haemorrhagic stroke) in trials of supplements
More prostate cancer in one large trial of a synthetic supplement
More heart failure in one trial in people with heart disease or diabetes
high.note: Too much vitamin E from food isn't a known problem; EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) found that only regular users of high-dose supplements are likely to go over the upper limit. Vitamin E at high amounts thins the blood by working against vitamin K, so the risk is higher with blood thinners or a shortage of vitamin K.

examples: Vegetable oils such as wheat germ, sunflower, safflower and rapeseed oil
Nuts and seeds: almonds, hazelnuts, sunflower seeds
Spinach and other green leafy vegetables
foodSources.note: Food tables often give vitamin E as alpha-tocopherol equivalents, which also count other tocopherols, so they can show more than the alpha-tocopherol that EFSA's values refer to.

forms.name: RRR-alpha-tocopherol (natural source, 'd-alpha')
forms.note: The form found in food. The liver keeps it in the blood more readily than the synthetic form, so labels may count it as more potent per milligram. 1 IU (international unit) is 0.67 mg.

forms.name: all-rac-alpha-tocopherol (synthetic, 'dl-alpha')
forms.note: A mix of eight mirror-image forms, of which the body keeps mainly half in the blood. 1 IU is 0.45 mg. The SELECT trial used this form as the acetate.

forms.name: Esters: alpha-tocopheryl acetate or succinate
forms.note: More stable on the shelf; the gut releases the vitamin from the ester. Can be natural or synthetic, so check the 'd' or 'dl' on the label.

forms.name: Mixed tocopherols and tocotrienols
forms.note: Contain gamma-tocopherol and other related compounds. EFSA's reference values and upper limit refer to alpha-tocopherol only, the form the body keeps; the other forms are less studied.

upperLimit.note: Tolerable upper intake level (UL) for alpha-tocopherol a day from all food and supplements, for adults including pregnant and breastfeeding women. EFSA reviewed it in 2024 and kept 300 mg, with impaired blood clotting and bleeding as the key risk. It covers all forms of alpha-tocopherol, natural and synthetic. It doesn't apply to people taking blood thinners or antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin, people treated to prevent another heart attack or stroke, or people who absorb vitamin K poorly. The intake values are adequate intakes (AI): EFSA couldn't work out an average need, so it used typical intakes of healthy people in the EU. They are guides for groups, not personal targets.

interactions.with: Blood thinners (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban and others)
interactions.note: Vitamin E at high amounts makes blood clot less well and can add to the bleeding risk of these medicines. EFSA's upper limit doesn't apply to people taking them. Discuss any vitamin E supplement with your doctor or pharmacist.

Vitamin E at high amounts makes blood clot less well and can add to the bleeding risk of these medicines. EFSA's upper limit doesn't apply to people taking them. Discuss any vitamin E supplement with your doctor or pharmacist.

interactions.with: Low vitamin K or poor vitamin K absorption
interactions.note: High amounts of vitamin E work against vitamin K, which the blood needs to clot. EFSA's upper limit doesn't apply to people who absorb vitamin K poorly.

interactions.with: A past heart attack or stroke
interactions.note: EFSA's upper limit doesn't apply to people treated to prevent another heart attack or stroke, and one trial in people with vascular disease found more heart failure with vitamin E. Ask your doctor first.
Because of the effect on clotting, tell the surgeon or dentist about vitamin E supplements before an operation.

interactions.with: Orlistat and conditions with poor fat absorption
interactions.note: Vitamin E is fat-soluble. Orlistat (a weight-loss medicine) and conditions that reduce fat absorption lower how much is absorbed. A doctor can check whether this matters.

cautions: Trial harms (bleeding strokes, prostate cancer) were seen with supplements, typically 400 IU a day or more, not with vitamin E from food.
Labels use IU or mg, and natural ('d-alpha') and synthetic ('dl-alpha') forms count differently.
Vitamin E is often added to multivitamins and 'antioxidant' products, so amounts can add up.
Unusual bruising or bleeding needs a doctor.

commonUses: May protect skin from UV damage

origin: Vitamin E is a group of fat-soluble compounds (tocopherols and tocotrienols) that protect the fats in cell membranes from damage. It comes mainly from vegetable oils, nuts and seeds.

Natural vitamin E (RRR-alpha-tocopherol) is extracted from vegetable oils; synthetic all-rac-alpha-tocopherol is manufactured and is less active per milligram. Mixed tocopherol and tocotrienol products are a different mix again.
dosage: EFSA's adequate intake is 13 mg a day for men and 11 mg for women. The upper limit for alpha-tocopherol from food and supplements is 300 mg a day. These are population values, not personal targets.
Amounts commonly used in supplements are about 15 to 50 mg a day. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.
Check the form and whether the label gives mg or IU, and avoid adding several products together. High amounts can matter with blood thinners (see below).

targets.label: Amount commonly used in studies and supplements (15 mg)
Amount commonly used in studies and supplements (50 mg, the top of the usual range)

foodAmounts.verdict: Yes. A handful of nuts or seeds or a little vegetable oil covers the adequate intake (about 50 g of almonds or 35 g of sunflower seeds). The 50 mg amount takes more: about 130 g of sunflower seeds, 200 g of almonds or 100 g of sunflower oil. Vitamin E from food comes with other compounds, and the amounts used in trials and supplements are often much larger, so food and supplements are different interventions.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the raw or boiled food named. Other foods, brands and fortified products differ. Vitamin E is shown as the table lists it; it does not split tocopherols from tocotrienols.
